page_title: IEEE Software - The Pragmatic Designer: Ur-Technical Debt

summary.title: IEEE Software - The Pragmatic Designer: Ur-Technical Debt
summary.one_liner: Learn Ward Cunningham's original meaning of technical debt (divergence between evolving understanding and code under iterative development) and why the term's broadened usage hinders choosing fixes.
takeaways: Ur-technical debt is the original meaning: code falls behind evolving understanding when building iteratively, and must be reworked.
Lumping hacks, novice code, architecture problems and lint warnings under 'technical debt' makes it harder to choose the right fix.
Iterative development creates this debt inherently, even with expert developers; it is not caused only by hacky code.
Static analysis tools largely cannot detect ur-technical debt; skilled developers must find it.
Teams need a real process for consolidating code (refactoring) or iterative development degrades into sedimentary accretion.
summary.summary: This IEEE Software column by George Fairbanks argues that the term technical debt has broadened beyond Ward Cunningham's 1992 meaning and proposes "ur-technical debt" for the original idea. The original idea is that iterative development makes code diverge from the developer's evolving understanding, which must be fixed through consolidation, much like paying interest. The author draws on Cunningham's original WyCash paper and his 2009 explanation, and argues that the debt metaphor does not help with decisions about when to fix debt. He also argues that static analysis tools cannot see this debt and that architecture debt is especially costly. The piece closes by recommending that different symptoms be treated with different remedies.
